claim: Israel was imposed on the land by outside powers, and the Jews took the land by force in 1948.

heard.who: Rashid Khalidi, historian, in The Hundred Years' War on Palestine (2020)
heard.quote: The resolution was another declaration of war, providing the international birth certificate for a Jewish state in most of what was still an Arab-majority land

answer: The idea came first from Britain, not from the Jews alone. In 1937 a British commission proposed splitting Palestine; Arabs rejected it, and Zionist leaders rejected its borders but kept talking. On 29 November 1947 the UN General Assembly recommended a Jewish state and an Arab state, by 33 votes to 13. The Jewish leadership accepted. The Arab Higher Committee and Arab states refused to be bound. Israel declared independence on 14 May 1948 and five Arab states sent armies in on 15 May. Israel ended the war holding more land than the plan gave it. Palestinian and Arab spokespeople call the vote unjust and the outcome conquest. The record shows a UN recommendation, one side that accepted it, one side that rejected it, and a war.

facts.text: In 1937 the British Peel Commission was the first to propose partitioning Palestine into an Arab state and a Jewish state.

sources.title: Peel Commission
sources.quote: In July 1937 the commission recommended the mandate be partitioned into an Arab state and a Jewish state, but the idea was ultimately rejected in 1938 as infeasible.

sources.publisher: United Nations (Conciliation Commission for Palestine, Secretariat)
sources.title: The Future of Arab Palestine and the Question of Partition (working paper)
sources.quote: the first proposal for the partition of Palestine was made in 1937 by the Peel Commission

facts.text: Both sides turned the Peel plan down. The Zionist Congress rejected its borders but empowered its leaders to negotiate a better plan.

sources.publisher: United Nations (Conciliation Commission for Palestine, Secretariat)
sources.title: The Future of Arab Palestine and the Question of Partition (working paper)
sources.quote: This plan was rejected by both Jews and Arabs.

sources.title: Twentieth Congress - Zurich, Switzerland (1937)
sources.quote: the congress decided to reject the specific borders recommended by the Peel Commission but empowered its executive to negotiate a more favorable plan for a Jewish state in Palestine

facts.text: UN General Assembly Resolution 181 of 29 November 1947 recommended a plan of partition with economic union: an Arab state, a Jewish state, and an international regime for Jerusalem.

sources.title: United Nations General Assembly Resolution 181
sources.quote: recommends to the United Kingdom, as the mandatory Power for Palestine, and to all other Members of the United Nations the adoption and implementation, with regard to the future government of Palestine, of the plan of partition with economic union

sources.title: United Nations Resolution 181
sources.quote: called for the partition of Palestine into Arab and Jewish states, with the city of Jerusalem as a corpus separatum

facts.text: The resolution passed with 33 votes in favour, 13 against and 10 abstentions.

sources.title: The Origins and Evolution of the Palestine Problem, Part II (1947-1977)
sources.quote: It received 33 votes in favour and 13 against with 10 abstentions

sources.title: United Nations Resolution 181
sources.quote: the resolution was passed with 33 votes in favor, 13 against, and 10 abstentions

facts.text: The Jewish community accepted the resolution; the Arab leadership rejected it and refused to recognise anything deriving from it.

sources.publisher: United Nations (Conciliation Commission for Palestine, Secretariat)
sources.title: The Future of Arab Palestine and the Question of Partition (working paper)
sources.quote: in accepting the partition plan, the Jews accepted indirectly the status of a future independent Arab state of Palestine

facts.text: On 14 May 1948 Israel's leaders issued a declaration of independence that cited the UN resolution and offered peace to neighbouring states.

facts.text: On 15 May 1948, as the British mandate ended, army units from Egypt, Transjordan, Iraq, Syria and Lebanon entered Palestine.

sources.title: 1948 Arab-Israeli War
sources.quote: on May 15, when the British Mandate came to an end, army units from Egypt, Transjordan (Jordan), Iraq, Syria, and Lebanon entered Palestine to fight on behalf of the Palestinian Arabs

facts.text: By the January 1949 ceasefire Israel held 77 percent of the Palestine region, more than the 56 percent the partition plan allotted to the Jewish state.

sources.title: 1948 Arab-Israeli War

contested: Khalidi argues the vote reflected the postwar balance of great powers (the US and USSR both voted yes, Britain abstained) and violated self-determination. Arab states argued the General Assembly had no power to partition a country; the UN Division for Palestinian Rights study records that they said they would not be bound. Supporters of the vote argued it was the best available option and that Jews, many of them refugees from Europe, also had a claim.

The UN Division for Palestinian Rights study says Jewish forces moved to occupy territory beyond the plan's lines when the mandate ended. That Division was set up to promote Palestinian rights, so its framing is one voice. Britannica gives the 77 percent versus 56 percent figures independently.

The Zionist Congress of 1937 rejected the specific Peel borders but did not reject partition in principle. Sources differ on how to summarise it: the UN secretariat paper says only that both sides rejected the plan.
not_claimed: This card does not claim the UN vote made the 1948 war or the later displacement of Palestinians right, wrong or inevitable.
It does not claim the vote was free of great-power pressure or that Palestinian Arabs were consulted in the way they wanted.
It does not claim Jewish forces took only land the plan gave them; see the 77 percent figure.
It does not say who fired first in the civil war that followed the vote.
